# Before you start

Work in this file. Write your answers where each question asks for them, render it, and hand in both files at the end of class:

+ this `.qmd` file, with your own name in the `author` field at the top
+ the `.html` file you get from rendering it

Leave `embed-resources: true` alone, so your `.html` opens on my machine without any extra files. Render one last time before you submit, so I know the document runs from top to bottom.

Everything here comes from lecture note 03-2. Three questions. Each has R parts, which need a code chunk showing both the code and its output, and plain-text parts, which need sentences rather than code. Writing an answer as plain text where a chunk was asked for does not count, even when the R is right.

Use the pipe. Every chain in this assignment should read as one `%>%` chain rather than a pile of intermediate objects, because that is the habit the lecture is trying to build.

# The data

We use `storms`, which comes with `dplyr` itself, so there is nothing extra to install. It is the NOAA record of Atlantic tropical storms and hurricanes, one row per storm per six-hour observation.

Run this first:

```{r}
library(dplyr)

storms
```

Useful columns for what follows:

+ `name`, `year`, `month`, `day`: which storm, and when the observation was taken
+ `status`: what the system was at that moment, for example `"hurricane"` or `"tropical storm"`
+ `category`: hurricane category, 1 to 5
+ `wind`: maximum sustained wind, in knots
+ `pressure`: air pressure at the storm's centre, in millibars. Lower means a stronger storm.

# Q1: choosing rows, choosing columns, ordering them

(a) In one chunk and one `%>%` chain, build an object called `hurr` that keeps only observations from `year` 2000 onwards whose `status` is `"hurricane"`, and only the columns `name`, `year`, `month`, `day`, `wind`, `pressure`, `category`, in that order. Print how many rows it has.

(b) In a new chunk, show the ten strongest observations in `hurr`, strongest first, by ordering on `wind`. Do not create a new object; start from `hurr` and pipe.

(c) `wind` is in knots and `pressure` is in millibars, and neither column name says so. In one chunk, rename them to `wind_kt` and `pressure_mb`, then move `wind_kt` to the front so it is the first column. Print the first few rows.

(d) In two or three sentences of plain text, explain what `%>%` does with the object on its left. Then say why `dplyr::filter(hurr, wind > 100)` and `hurr %>% dplyr::filter(wind > 100)` give the same answer.

# Q2: creating and recoding columns

(a) One knot is 0.5144 metres per second. In one chunk, add a column `wind_ms` holding the wind speed in metres per second, rounded to one decimal place, and move `wind` and `wind_ms` to the front so you can see them side by side.

(b) A hurricane counts as **major** at 96 knots or more. In one chunk, add a column `is_major` that reads `"major"` for those observations and `"not major"` for the rest, then report how many observations fall in each group. Use the counting approach from the lecture: group, then summarize with `n()`.

(c) In one chunk, add a column `pressure_class` with three values: `"very low"` below 950 mb, `"low"` from 950 up to but not including 980, and `"moderate or high"` at 980 and above. Report how many observations fall in each class. Two nested `ifelse()` calls would work, but there is a function meant for exactly this, so use it.

(d) In two or three sentences of plain text, say when you would reach for `ifelse()` and when you would reach for the function you used in (c), and what goes wrong if you try to write three categories with a single `ifelse()`.

# Q3: grouped summaries, and the trap in them

(a) In one chunk, produce one row per `year` giving the number of hurricane observations, the mean `wind`, and the highest `wind` that year. Name all three columns yourself.

(b) In one chunk, produce one row per storm per year, giving that storm's peak wind and how many observations it has. Save it as `peak`. Print it, and look carefully at the line just under the tibble dimensions.

(c) The object you just printed reports something on a `Groups:` line. In two or three sentences of plain text, say which grouping variable is still attached to `peak`, why `summarize()` left it there, and what would go wrong if you now piped `peak` into `dplyr::mutate(share = n_obs / sum(n_obs))` without thinking about it.

(d) In one chunk, remove the leftover grouping from `peak` and then show the ten storms with the highest peak wind, strongest first.
